raw_response:
Looking at my land and what I know, it is not complicated. My family has farmed this ground for decades. In Quzhou, everybody grows winter wheat and summer maize on the same fields, one after the other. That is what the land is for. The soil here on the North China Plain suits it, the water is there — we pump from the well — and I know exactly what to do because I have been doing it since I was helping my father at fifteen.

I have about 8 mu. I will plant all of it to wheat starting in October, then after the June harvest I turn straight around and plant maize on the same ground. No fallow, no experimenting. My cousin tried growing vegetables a few years back — too much work, prices crashed, he lost money. I will not do that.

For wheat, I will use the Shimai variety — it does well here, the county extension people hand it out and my neighbor gets good yields with it. Not the traditional seeds my grandfather saved; those yield less. For maize, I buy郑单958 hybrid seed from the township supply co-op every year. It is reliable.

Fertilizer — I put down compound fertilizer at planting for the base, then urea when the wheat is jointing in March. For maize I throw urea on at the big-bell stage. I probably use more nitrogen than I should but I am not going to risk a thin crop. For water, wheat needs three times: the winter freeze-in irrigation in November to protect the roots, jointing water in late March, and grain-filling water in May. Maize I irrigate if it looks dry at silking, maybe once or twice depending on the rain that summer.

I spray herbicide on the wheat in winter when the weeds come up, and fungicide at heading to stop rust — I lost part of a crop to rust eight years ago and I have not skipped that spray since. For maize I spray once for pests around pollination.

Tillage is rotary both times. I rent the tractor from the village machine cooperative. Ploughing is too expensive and my soil does not need it.
